nameStory: The zebra spider gets its striking name from its bold black and white stripes that look just like a zebra's coat! The scientific name is equally dramatic — 'Salticus' means 'jump' in Latin, while 'scenicus' comes from Greek meaning 'theatrical,' perfectly capturing this little performer's flashy appearance and acrobatic leaps.
description: This tiny jumping spider is like a miniature zebra that can leap! Only about the size of a pencil eraser, the zebra jumping spider sports distinctive black and white stripes across its compact, fuzzy body. Unlike web-spinning spiders, these athletic hunters actively stalk their prey with cat-like movements and can jump several times their own body length. They're one of the most commonly seen jumping spiders across New England.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Bold black and white zebra-like stripes run across the body, creating a pattern so distinctive it looks almost painted on

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a row give it an almost cute, curious expression — the two middle eyes are noticeably larger

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and stocky like a tiny tank, with a fuzzy texture and short, sturdy legs built for jumping rather than web-spinning

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions like a cat stalking prey, often turning to face you directly when approached — no web to be found

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to fit comfortably on a dime, typically about 4-7mm long including legs

habitat: Look for zebra jumping spiders on sun-warmed vertical surfaces like fence posts, tree bark, stone walls, and the sides of buildings throughout New England. They love basking on rough-textured surfaces where they can easily grip with their fuzzy feet. You'll often spot them on wooden decks, rock walls, and even house siding on sunny days.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active on warm, sunny days. Look for them sunbathing on south-facing walls and fence posts.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with adults actively hunting and mating. Males perform elaborate courtship dances, waving their striped legs like tiny semaphore flags.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs in protected crevices before adults die off. Young spiders may still be active on warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Juveniles overwinter in bark crevices, under loose siding, or in other protected spots, emerging only on unusually warm winter days.

funFact: Zebra jumping spiders have better color vision than humans — they can see into the ultraviolet spectrum and use this superpower to spot prey and identify mates with hidden UV patterns we can't even see!
confusionNotes: The zebra pattern is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other spiders, but other jumping spiders might cause confusion. Remember: if it has obvious black and white stripes like a zebra, you've found your spider — other jumpers have spots, bands, or solid colors instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'zebra spiders,' they're actually more closely related to peacock spiders than to any African mammals! The theatrical courtship displays of males rival any Broadway show, with leg-waving dances that would make a choreographer proud.
compareHints: While there are no other Salticus species in our New England dataset, zebra jumping spiders can be distinguished from other jumping spiders by their unique zebra-stripe pattern — most other jumpers have spots, solid colors, or different banding patterns. Their compact, tank-like build also sets them apart from the more elongated or colorful jumping spiders you might encounter.
